raw_text:
### Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, causing substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. For decades, pharmacological management centered on blocking the overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. However, the introduction of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) marked a significant paradigm shift. Sacubitril/valsartan (originally known as LCZ696) represents a first-in-class agent that simultaneously inhibits neprilysin via its active metabolite sacubitrilat and blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor via valsartan [1]. Neprilysin inhibition prevents the degradation of beneficial vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, and anti-fibrotic effects. Concurrently, AT1 receptor blockade mitigates the harmful consequences of angiotensin II elevation that would otherwise result from neprilysin inhibition alone [1].

### Clinical Efficacy in HFrEF
The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. In this double-blind trial, 8,399 patients with chronic HFrEF (LVEF $\le$ 40%) were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan or the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor enalapril. The trial was terminated early due to overwhelming benefit, showing a 20% reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization in the sacubitril/valsartan group [1]. Subsequent analyses confirmed that ARNI therapy significantly reduced cardiovascular mortality [17], slowed clinical progression [9], lowered recurrent HF hospitalizations [24], and improved health-related quality of life [29]. 

These clinical benefits were consistent across various patient subgroups, including those stratified by age [25], baseline risk [27], background HF medications [26], and background beta-blocker dosing [28]. The treatment effect was also independent of prior enalapril equivalent doses [23]. Furthermore, modeling studies have projected that comprehensive disease-modifying therapy incorporating ARNI can add several years of life for HFrEF patients [14].

### Cardiac Remodeling and Biomarkers
The physiological mechanisms underlying the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan have been extensively evaluated through cardiac imaging and biomarker studies. The PROVE-HF trial demonstrated that initiating sacubitril/valsartan led to significant reductions in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which correlated strongly with improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and other indices of reverse cardiac remodeling [4]. Complementing these findings, the EVALUATE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan improved aortic stiffness and decreased left ventricular end-diastolic volume index compared to enalapril over 12 weeks of treatment [5].

### Acute Decompensated Heart Failure and Initiation Strategies
Transitioning patients to sacubitril/valsartan during or immediately after hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) has emerged as an essential therapeutic strategy. The PIONEER-HF trial randomized hospitalized HFrEF patients stabilized after ADHF to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril, demonstrating a significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP and a reduction in serious clinical outcomes, such as rehospitalization [2, 18]. The TRANSITION trial supported these findings, demonstrating that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either in-hospital or shortly after discharge was both safe and feasible [8]. Safe titration protocols were further validated by the TITRATION study, which outlined strategies for optimizing doses in both treatment-naive and experienced patients [30].

### Preserved and Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction
The utility of sacubitril/valsartan has also been investigated across the ejection fraction spectrum. The phase II PARAMOUNT trial first demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan reduced NT-proBNP to a greater extent than valsartan alone in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [21]. The subsequent phase III PARAGON-HF trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan in patients with LVEF $\ge$ 45% [3]. Although it narrowly missed the pre-specified statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (rate ratio 0.87, p=0.059) [3], a prespecified pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF revealed significant clinical benefits extending to patients with ejection fractions below the normal range (specifically, up to ~57-60%), with a particularly pronounced benefit observed in women [19].

### Special Populations, Tolerability, and Guidelines
ARNI therapy offers distinct advantages in renal and metabolic profiles. In PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan preserved renal function and slowed the decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to enalapril or valsartan [10, 22]. These renal benefits are especially prominent in patients with type 2 diabetes [15]. Moreover, sacubitril/valsartan has been shown to improve long-term glycemic control, as evidenced by significant reductions in HbA1c levels [16]. In patients with chronic kidney disease without heart failure, the UK-HARP-III trial confirmed its favorable safety profile and comparable effects on renal function compared to irbesartan [20]. 

Despite these benefits, clinical management requires caution regarding symptomatic hypotension, although rates of hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction are lower than with traditional RAAS inhibitors [11, 25]. However, its efficacy in advanced NYHA class IV HFrEF remains limited, as the LIFE trial showed no significant benefit over valsartan in this cohort [7]. Additionally, in the post-myocardial infarction setting, the PARADISE-MI trial did not show a significant reduction in CV death or HF events compared to ramipril, though it remained safe and well-tolerated [6].

Based on this extensive body of evidence, current international guidelines have elevated the status of sacubitril/valsartan. The 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines [12] and the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America (AHA/ACC/HFSA) guidelines [13] now recommend ARNI as a Class I, first-line therapy for patients with HFrEF to reduce morbidity and mortality, either as a replacement for or in lieu of an ACE inhibitor or ARB. Guidelines also suggest its use in patients with HFmrEF and select HFpEF phenotypes to help manage symptoms and reduce hospitalizations.
